_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 4 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 6 Inputs, Outputs and Parts. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The five chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order (inputs to a program; planning an object; testing part by part; fix then run again; debugging systematically), in the lesson's own words and with the lesson's own objects: the cat, the door, the score sign, and the three-part program whose part 2 spins when it should jump. The hardware in the first chapter is the lesson kit's own laptop and tablet figures, rung part by part; the blocks in every program box are the kit's own BLOCKS, and the counts (two jumps, three moves right) come from ART.program.expand rather than from a copy in the film.
title: Inputs, Outputs and Parts
subtitle: Grade 4 Computing
objectives: Know how to develop programs that produce different outputs from different inputs.
Know how to plan the instructions for objects within programs, including identifying inputs and outputs.
Know how to test different parts of a program systematically, to identify and debug errors.

beats.say: Press A and the cat jumps. Press B and the very same cat spins.
One sprite, two inputs, two scripts, two different outputs.
A program can wait for an input: a key, a button, a click on a sprite.
Press A. That input has a script of its own, and the cat jumps.
Press B. A different script runs, and the same cat spins.
Click the cat and it says hello. Press the space bar and it hides.
Four inputs, four scripts, four different outputs, from one sprite.
Before you build an object, plan it. What is its input? What is its output?
The cat's input is the A key. Its output is a jump.
The door's input is the player walking into it.
Its output is the door opening and playing a creak.
The score sign waits for the ball to hit the goal, then adds one.

at.ball: the ball to hit the goal

beats.say: Nothing happens without an input, so plan both.
This program is in three named parts: the reset, the jumps, the greeting.
Run part one on its own. The cat goes home. That part is fine.
Run part two. The cat spins, and we wanted two jumps.
So the bug is in part two, and nowhere else in the program.
Testing one part at a time tells you where, instead of leaving you to guess.
Fix the block in the part that failed. Take out spin, put in jump.
Now run part two again. Two jumps. That part passes.
Only when every part passes does the whole program pass.
The next program had two bugs, hiding in two different parts.
Part by part found them one at a time, which is far easier.
There is a bad way to find a bug: changing things until it works.
That sometimes works, and it teaches you nothing at all.
The good way is debugging systematically. Split the program into parts.
Run one part. Check its result against what you expected.
Move on only when that part is right. The error has nowhere to hide.

at.moveon: Move on only when that part is right

beats.say: Each input runs its own script, so a different input gives a different output.
Plan an object by naming its input and its output before you build.
Test one part at a time. The part that fails holds the bug.

at.test: Test one part at a time

beats.say: Fix that block, run the part again, and the error has nowhere to hide.
